items.text: Significant policy infrastructure already exists from the core-runtime item: Policy CRUD API (all endpoints wired), SQLite store with policy_rules/violations/circuit_breaker_overrides tables, evaluator (access-only), broadcaster (incremental events), and receiver-side middleware (access-only). The work is extending these existing foundations, not greenfield.

items.topic: Schema: flat columns vs rule_data JSON blob
items.context: The spec describes the schema with a single `rule_data TEXT as JSON` column for rule-type-specific config. The existing implementation uses individual columns (max_requests, window_seconds, burst_allowance, failure_threshold, cooldown_seconds, success_threshold) which provides compile-time type safety and queryability. Changing to JSON would require rewriting all store methods and handler validation.

options.label: Keep current flat columns
options.rationale: Already working, type-safe, queryable via SQL, no migration needed. Slight denormalization (access rules have unused rate-limit columns) but SQLite handles this fine at current scale.

options.label: Migrate to rule_data JSON blob
options.rationale: Matches spec exactly, more flexible for future rule types, but loses SQL queryability and requires rewriting store layer + migration of existing data.

items.topic: Access control: specificity scoring vs manual priority
items.context: The spec describes auto-computed specificity scoring (exact=3pts, prefix glob=2pts, wildcard=1pt, summed across source+target+action, max 9, ties broken by creation time). The current implementation uses a manual `priority` column set by the API caller, with rules evaluated highest-priority-first. Auto-scoring removes admin burden but limits override control.

options.label: Auto-computed specificity scoring per spec
options.rationale: Exactly matches the spec. Scoring is deterministic and predictable—more specific rules always win without admin tuning. Compute score on create/update and store in the priority column.

options.label: Keep manual priority
options.rationale: Simpler, already working, gives admins explicit control. But requires operators to understand and set correct priorities for every rule.

options.label: Hybrid: auto-score as default, allow manual override
options.rationale: Best of both worlds but adds complexity. Auto-compute unless the caller explicitly sets a priority value.

items.topic: Rate limiter state storage: in-memory vs SQLite
items.context: Token bucket rate limiting needs per-rule state (tokens_remaining, last_refill_time). This state is hot-path (checked on every request in the middleware) and ephemeral (losing it on restart just means a brief burst window). Two main options for where state lives.

options.label: In-memory with sync.Mutex per rule
options.rationale: Fastest path—no disk I/O on every request. State resets on restart (acceptable: just means full bucket). Simple Go maps. This is for the receiver-side middleware cache.

options.label: SQLite table for rate limit state
options.rationale: Survives restarts, centrally visible for debugging. But adds disk I/O to every request evaluation, and the middleware is meant to be a local cache, not a database client.

items.topic: Policy push: incremental events vs full snapshot
items.context: The spec says 'push full policy ruleset snapshot to all connected SSE clients for atomic cache replacement (no partial state, no version tracking).' The current broadcaster sends incremental events (created/updated/deleted) which the middleware applies individually. Incremental is more bandwidth-efficient but can drift if an event is missed.

options.label: Full snapshot push per spec
options.rationale: Matches spec. Atomic replacement means no drift risk. At current scale (dozens of rules), the payload is small. Simple to implement: serialize all enabled rules on any change, broadcast as single SSE event.

options.label: Keep incremental events
options.rationale: Already implemented. More bandwidth-efficient at scale. But requires the receiver to handle every possible event type correctly, and a missed event causes permanent drift until reconnection.

options.label: Snapshot on connect, incremental after
options.rationale: Best of both: full state on connect (no drift), efficient updates after. More complex to implement correctly.

items.topic: Middleware scope: server-side evaluator vs receiver-side middleware
items.context: The spec says 'receiver-side enforcement middleware' — three middleware layers (access, rate limit, circuit breaker) that run in the receiving scenario's HTTP chain using locally-cached policies. The existing code has BOTH: a server-side Evaluator (in internal/policy/evaluator.go, queries DB directly) used by the POST /policies/evaluate endpoint, AND a receiver-side PolicyMiddleware (in internal/middleware/policy.go) using cached rules. This item needs to clarify: are we building the three-layer enforcement into the receiver-side middleware (which other scenarios import), or into the server-side evaluator, or both?

options.label: Three-layer enforcement in receiver-side middleware only
options.rationale: Matches spec exactly. The middleware runs in other scenarios' HTTP chains, enforcing access+rate-limit+circuit-breaker with locally-cached rules. The server-side evaluator stays as-is for the /evaluate API endpoint (dry-run / testing).

options.label: Three-layer enforcement in both server-side and receiver-side
options.rationale: Full parity between the evaluate API and actual enforcement. But duplicates logic and the server-side evaluator was designed for point-in-time checks, not stateful rate limiting.
